title: Maximum Sum Circular Subarray
directAnswer: The best circular subarray is either non-wrapping (plain Kadane maximum) or wrapping. A wrapping subarray equals the total sum minus some inner subarray, so the best wrap = total − (minimum subarray sum). Return max(maxKadane, total − minKadane), but guard the all-negative case: if maxKadane < 0, every element is negative and 'total − min' would wrongly suggest the empty subarray, so just return maxKadane. One pass, O(n) time, O(1) space.

remember.pattern: Kadane twice — max subarray and total minus min subarray
remember.formula:
maxSum = Kadane_max(nums)
minSum = Kadane_min(nums)
total  = sum(nums)
if maxSum < 0: return maxSum   # all negative
return max(maxSum, total - minSum)
rules: The answer is the better of two cases: a **non-wrapping** subarray (plain Kadane) or a **wrapping** one.
A wrapping subarray = **total − (the inner non-wrapping subarray it excludes)**, so its max is `total − minSubarraySum`.
**Guard the all-negative array**: if the max subarray sum is `< 0`, return it directly — `total − minSum` collapses to the empty subarray (value 0), which is illegal.
Run **two Kadanes in one pass**: track running max and running min simultaneously while accumulating the total.
The subarray must be **non-empty**; the empty-subarray trap is exactly what the all-negative guard prevents.
whenToUse: Maximum/minimum subarray sum where the array wraps around (circular)
You already know Kadane and the array is a ring buffer
A 'best contiguous segment' problem with end-to-front continuity
Any problem reducible to 'total minus the worst middle chunk'
antiSignals: Array is linear, not circular → plain Kadane is enough
You need the subarray indices, not just the sum → track boundaries during Kadane
Elements can be reused / it's a subsequence → different DP
You need max product, not sum → Maximum Product Subarray (track min and max factors)
remember.takeaway: Maximum Sum Circular Subarray is Kadane with a twist: the wrapping case is just total minus the minimum subarray. Running max- and min-Kadane together in one pass — plus the all-negative guard — is the whole trick. The 'total − worst middle' complement idea recurs whenever a structure wraps.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you realize a circular subarray is either non-wrapping (Kadane) or wrapping (= total − minimum subarray), and whether you catch the all-negative edge case that the complement trick breaks on.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Forgetting the all-negative guard, so total − minSum returns 0 (the empty subarray) instead of the largest single negative element.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Derive the wrapping case as 'total minus the min subarray', run both Kadanes in a single pass, and proactively call out the all-negative edge case before the interviewer does.

problemStatement:
Given a ***circular integer array*** `nums` of length `n`, return the **maximum possible sum of a non-empty subarray** of `nums`.

A *circular array* means the end of the array connects to the beginning: formally, the next element of `nums[i]` is `nums[(i + 1) % n]`.

A *subarray* may only include each element of the fixed buffer `nums` **at most once**: formally, for a subarray `nums[i], nums[i+1], ..., nums[j]`, there does not exist `i <= k1, k2 <= j` with `k1 % n == k2 % n`.
constraints: The subarray must be non-empty and use each buffer index at most once
understanding: Find the largest sum of a contiguous run of elements, where 'contiguous' may wrap from the end of the array back to the front. No element is used twice. The wrap is the only difference from classic Maximum Subarray (Kadane).

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the subarray wrap around the end?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — that's the whole point. A run like nums[n-1], nums[0], nums[1] is valid. Without wrapping this is plain Maximum Subarray.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Must the subarray be non-empty?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. This matters enormously: when every element is negative the answer is the largest (least negative) single element, not 0.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can an element be used more than once?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. Even though it's circular, each buffer index appears at most once, so a wrapping subarray can't be longer than n.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are all elements possibly negative?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, and that's the key edge case. The total-minus-min trick must be guarded, or it returns 0 (the empty subarray) instead of the max element.

examples.explanation: The non-wrapping subarray [3] gives 3 — wrapping doesn't help here.
The wrapping subarray [5, (wrap), 5] sums to 10, beating the best non-wrapping run (5-3+5 = 7).
All negative — the answer is the largest single element, -2. The total-minus-min trick must NOT return 0.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Try Every Circular Subarray
approaches.whenToMention: Open with this to frame the search space, then flag it as too slow for n = 3·10⁴ before pivoting to Kadane.
hints: A circular subarray is fixed by a start index and a length (1 to n). How would you sum each candidate?
For every start i, extend a running sum across up to n elements, wrapping the index with (i + k) % n, and track the best sum seen.
Reset and repeat for each start. Every non-empty circular subarray is covered exactly once.
approaches.complexityReasoning: There are n starting positions and up to n lengths each, with O(1) work per extension (using modular indexing), giving O(n²) total time and O(1) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
The most direct reading: a circular subarray is determined by where it starts and how long it is. So fix each start index `i`, then grow the subarray one element at a time — using `(i + k) % n` to wrap past the end — accumulating a running sum and recording the maximum.

**Why this covers wrapping for free.** Modular indexing means a subarray starting near the end naturally continues into the front of the array. Capping the length at `n` enforces the 'each index at most once' rule. No special wrap logic is needed — the `% n` does it.

**Why this is the honest baseline.** It makes 'every possible circular subarray' literally executable and is trivially correct, which is exactly what you want to state before optimizing. It also handles the non-empty requirement automatically since every candidate has length ≥ 1.

**Why we don't ship it.** With `n` up to `3·10⁴`, `O(n²)` is ~900 million operations — too slow. And it's wasteful: as the start advances, the sums it computes overlap heavily with the previous start's work. That overlap, plus the classic Maximum Subarray connection, points straight at Kadane.
approaches.insight: Recomputing overlapping running sums for each start is the redundancy Kadane removes in the linear case. Recognizing that the circular problem is 'Maximum Subarray, but the buffer wraps' is the bridge: solve the two halves (wrap / no-wrap) with the linear tool you already trust.

approaches.name: Standard Kadane — Non-Wrapping Only (Building Block)
approaches.whenToMention: Establish Kadane as the tool, then immediately show it misses the wrapping case (e.g. [5,-3,5]) — motivating the full solution.
hints: Recall Maximum Subarray: a running sum that resets whenever it would do better starting fresh. curMax = max(x, curMax + x).
Track the best curMax ever seen. This finds the optimal NON-wrapping subarray in one pass.
Now test it on [5,-3,5]: Kadane gives 7, but the true circular answer is 10. What case is it missing?
approaches.complexityReasoning: A single pass with O(1) work per element → O(n) time, O(1) space. It just doesn't cover wraps yet.
approaches.explanation:
Kadane's algorithm is the linear core. Maintain a running subarray sum `curMax`; at each element decide whether to extend the current subarray or start fresh at the current element: `curMax = max(x, curMax + x)`. Track the largest `curMax` seen in `maxSum`. That value is the best *non-wrapping* subarray sum.

**Why this is the right building block.** The circular problem is just Maximum Subarray with one extra case (the wrap). Establishing the linear answer first mirrors how you'd reason on a whiteboard and gives half the final answer directly — the non-wrapping candidate.

**Where it falls short.** Consider `[5, -3, 5]`. Kadane finds `5 - 3 + 5 = 7` (the whole array) or just `5`. But the best circular subarray takes the last `5`, wraps around, and grabs the first `5` for `10`. Kadane alone cannot see this because it only considers contiguous runs in the *linear* array — it never wraps.

**The fix this motivates.** A wrapping subarray is a suffix plus a prefix — i.e. the entire array *minus* a contiguous middle chunk. To maximize the wrap, minimize that excluded middle. So the full solution runs Kadane a second time to find the *minimum* subarray, and computes `total − minSum`. The next approach combines both into one pass.
approaches.insight: Kadane's decision 'extend or restart' (curMax = max(x, curMax + x)) is the atomic move of all max-subarray problems. Seeing precisely what it CAN'T do — wrap around — is what tells you to add the complementary 'total minus min subarray' case rather than inventing something exotic.

approaches.name: Two-Case Kadane — max(Kadane, total − minKadane) (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Frame it as 'the best subarray either doesn't wrap (Kadane) or it does — and a wrap is total minus the minimum subarray', then call out the all-negative guard.
hints: Split into two cases. Case 1: the best subarray doesn't wrap → plain Kadane max. Case 2: it wraps.
A wrapping subarray is the whole array minus a contiguous middle chunk. To maximize the wrap, minimize that chunk → total − (minimum subarray sum).

Run max-Kadane and min-Kadane together while summing the total. Answer = max(maxSum, total − minSum). But if maxSum < 0, every element is negative — return maxSum, because total − minSum would be the empty subarray (0).
approaches.complexityReasoning: One pass maintaining running max, running min, and the total — all O(1) per element → O(n) time and O(1) space. No second array, no recursion.
approaches.explanation:
Every circular subarray is exactly one of two shapes, so we compute the best of each and take the larger.

**Case 1 — the best subarray doesn't wrap.** This is plain Maximum Subarray: Kadane gives `maxSum`, the best contiguous run within the linear array.

**Case 2 — the best subarray wraps around the end.** A wrapping subarray consists of a suffix `nums[i..n-1]` joined with a prefix `nums[0..j]`. Equivalently, it's the *entire* array minus the contiguous middle chunk `nums[j+1..i-1]` that it leaves out. So `wrappingSum = total − middleSum`. To make the wrap as large as possible, we make the excluded middle as small as possible — i.e. `total − minSubarraySum`, where `minSubarraySum` is the *minimum* contiguous subarray sum (a second Kadane, minimizing instead of maximizing).

**Why both Kadanes run in a single pass.** The max-Kadane recurrence `curMax = max(x, curMax + x)` and the min-Kadane recurrence `curMin = min(x, curMin + x)` are independent and can be updated together as we also accumulate `total`. One loop, three running quantities, O(1) memory.

**The critical all-negative guard.** If every element is negative, the minimum subarray *is the whole array*, so `total − minSum = 0` — which corresponds to excluding everything, i.e. the **empty** subarray. But the problem demands a non-empty subarray. Detect this exactly when `maxSum < 0` (the best non-wrapping subarray is itself negative, which only happens when all elements are negative). In that case the true answer is `maxSum` — the largest (least negative) single element — so we return it directly and never consult the wrap case. For `[-3, -2, -3]`, `maxSum = -2` and the guard correctly returns `-2` instead of `0`.

**Putting it together.** `if maxSum < 0: return maxSum; else return max(maxSum, total − minSum)`. The two cases are exhaustive, each solved by an O(n) Kadane, and the guard handles the one degenerate input — a clean, complete O(n)/O(1) solution.
approaches.insight: The wrap-equals-complement idea — 'a wrapping segment is the total minus an inner segment' — converts a scary circular problem into two ordinary linear ones. Whenever a structure wraps and you want the best wrapping piece, ask 'what's the worst piece I could remove?' The all-negative guard is the reminder that complement tricks can silently admit the empty set.

pitfalls: Omitting the all-negative guard — returns 0 for arrays like [-3,-2,-3] instead of the max element.
Initializing maxSum/minSum to 0 instead of nums[0] — corrupts both Kadanes on all-negative or all-positive inputs.
Computing total − minSum where minSum spans the whole array without the guard — that's the empty-subarray bug.

commonMistakes: Forgetting the all-negative guard — total − minSum returns 0 (empty subarray) instead of the largest element.
Using only plain Kadane — misses wrapping subarrays like [5,-3,5] → 10.
Initializing the running max/min to 0 rather than nums[0] — breaks all-negative and all-positive arrays.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Missing the all-negative guard
commonMistakesDetailed.why: When every element is negative, the minimum subarray is the entire array, so total − minSum = 0 — the empty subarray, which is forbidden. Without the guard you return 0 instead of the max (least-negative) element.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Plain Kadane ignores wrapping
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Standard Maximum Subarray only considers contiguous runs in the linear array, so it can't capture a suffix+prefix wrap. You must add the total − minSubarray case.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: return max_sum  # only the non-wrapping case

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong initial values for the running extrema
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Seeding maxSum or minSum at 0 assumes an empty subarray is allowed and biases all-negative / all-positive inputs. Seed them with nums[0] and start the running curMax/curMin at 0.

patternNote: Kadane with a complement twist. Recognize it when 'maximum subarray' meets a circular buffer: the answer is max(plain Kadane, total − minimum subarray), guarded against the all-negative empty-subarray case. The 'total minus the worst middle' idea reappears wherever a structure wraps; the dual max/min Kadane recurs in Maximum Product Subarray.
